transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-20
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Recording ID: ff-20250520-8372

Summary (auto): Quick technical deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategy for Metra's multi-tenant assistant workload. Discussed cache key design, hit rates, eviction, multi-tenant isolation, VPC/on-prem constraints, and benchmarking plan. Agreed next steps: share docs, run benchmark, provide workload traces.

Topics: prefix caching, KV cache hit-rate, cache keys & hashing, tenant isolation, cache TTLs, eviction, batching interactions, quantization implications, VPC/on-prem cache placement, encryption/KMS.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Sophia: alright everyone, thanks for joining, I'm sophia from Redwood Inference, i'm the AE on this account, i'll hand off to carlos in a bit for the deep part but we want to understand metra's target hit rates and concerns around multi-tenant safety for prefix caching.
[00:00:18] Angela: yeah thanks, we've been looking at ways to reduce per-token cost and latency. our main ask: can we safely cache common system prompts & prefixes across tenants without leakage, what are hit-rate expectations, and how does this work on our VPC/on-prem pilot.
[00:00:32] Carlos: great question. i'm carlos, solutions engineer. quick overview: Redwood supports prefix/prompt caching via the KV cache layer and an optional shared prefix cache. keys can be tenant-scoped or global depending on policy. the typical approach is to namespace keys with tenant id and a hash of the prefix text so you get strong isolation.
[00:00:50] Ravi: when you say namespace, do you mean the cache stores separate buckets per tenant or you prefix the key string? what's the risk of collisions?
[00:00:58] Carlos: we usually do both: logical buckets + hashed keys. in practice we do key = sha256(tenant_id || ":" || prefix_text || ":" || model_hash || ":" || quant_profile). that reduces accidental collisions; collisions are astronomically unlikely with sha256 but we also add a signer in enterprise mode so the cache entries are cryptographically bound to tenant and model.
[00:01:20] Jon: signer? is that an HMAC with KMS? how does that affect performance?
[00:01:27] Carlos: it's an HMAC that's optional for on-prem or VPC setups where you want extra tamper-proofing. compute overhead for generating/verifying is microseconds per entry; negligible compared to token generation time. for hosted Redwood we use internal signing to prevent cross-tenant access.
[00:01:42] [00:01:45] Angela: ok makes sense. what about hit rates—what should we expect for a typical assistant workload with many similar prompts but per-user personalization?
[00:01:52] Carlos: great, so hit rates are workload dependent. for 80% of conversational assistants we see 40-70% prefix cache hit rates if you cache common system prompts, instruction templates, and shared few-shot examples. if you can normalize prompts (strip user-specific tokens, canonicalize placeholders) you'll push the hit rate up. we recommended aiming for a 60% hit-rate target for the pilot.
[00:02:12] Ravi: normalization — how do you suggest handling personalization tokens like {user_name} or session ids inside prompts?
[00:02:18] Carlos: pattern is to replace those with stable placeholders at the prompt-prep layer. Redwood has a preprocessor hook (a lightweight transform) you can run before hashing keys. that preprocessor can remove ephemeral tokens, canonicalize timestamps, etc. we can share the template.
[00:02:30] Priya: are there any gotchas with batching? if you increase batching for throughput does that affect cacheability?
[00:02:36] Carlos: batching is orthogonal but interacts with latency SLOs. if you batch many requests that share prefixes, you get higher amortized cost savings. however large batches increase P99 latency. for Metra's latency SLO we recommend adaptive batching with per-route configs: small batch sizes for low-latency routes, larger for background reranking. cache hit-rate improves with more repeated prefixes in the batch.
[00:02:58] [00:03:05] Angela: quantization — does 8-bit or 4-bit quantization change whether a cached prefix is compatible? i.e., do you need to include quant profile in the cache key?
[00:03:12] Carlos: yes, include quant_profile in the key. different quant settings can change model outputs slightly because of kernel selection; to be safe we include model_hash + quant_profile. Redwood can automatically recommend quant profiles for your workload; we'll include the recommended defaults in the doc.
[00:03:27] Ravi: what's the behavior if there's a cache miss? do you recompute prefix KV and store it, or is there a warm pool?
[00:03:34] Carlos: on miss we compute and populate the KV cache for subsequent requests. for high-priority prefixes we support proactive/pre-warm strategies: you can prepopulate common prefixes at deployment or during off-peak. we also have a small shared warm pool that can be filled by background jobs.
[00:03:49] Jon: eviction strategy? memory budgeting across tenants? we can't have one tenant blow up the cache.
[00:03:55] Carlos: per-tenant quotas + LRU per-namespace is the standard. you set a memory cap per tenant and a global cap. we expose metrics for bytes used by prefix cache per-tenant and eviction counts. for Dedicated and Private deployments you can configure strict caps and alerts.
[00:04:10] [00:04:18] Angela: multi-tenant safety: if we accidentally reuse a prefix intended for tenant A in tenant B because of a misconfigured key, what's the risk and detection?
[00:04:25] Sophia: i'll add: Redwood's default is tenant-scoped keys. cross-tenant reuse would only occur if someone intentionally configures a shared cache policy. for extra protection we log cache-origin headers and audit logs; SOC2 customers can enable immutable audit trails.
[00:04:39] Carlos: detection is via mismatch checks: we include tenant id in the signed metadata and the runtime rejects entries that don't verify. telemetry will show unexpected hit patterns. in practice we've seen misconfig only in manual copy/paste configs and we can run a linter on your infra-as-code to catch that.
[00:04:55] Ravi: metrics—what should we look at during the pilot?
[00:05:00] Carlos: key metrics: prefix cache hit rate (by route), average token-level cost reduction, fill rate, eviction rate, miss latency delta (time to compute and store), and end-to-end P50/P95/P99 latency. also track model divergence/regression by sampling outputs before/after enabling cache to catch subtle quality shifts.
[00:05:20] Priya: model divergence — you mean evals against prompts? how do we detect if caching changes output quality?
[00:05:26] Carlos: yes, you run A/B evals: route X uses cache, route Y bypasses cache for sampled requests and compare outputs via your eval metrics. Redwood Optimize can run regression alerts on a small eval set. we recommend a 1 week baseline then gradual rollout (canary 5%, 25%, 100%).
[00:05:41] [00:05:50] Angela: VPC/on-prem specifics: we want the cache to live inside our VPC, encrypted at rest, and with KMS keys we control. is that supported?
[00:05:58] Carlos: yes for Private deployments we run the control plane in your VPC and the cache can either be co-located (recommended) or use a customer-managed Redis cluster. for strongest security we support envelope encryption with your KMS/HSM; Redwood's runtime will fetch keys on startup using IAM roles. for on-prem, you can run the cache as a local service behind your network controls.
[00:06:19] Jon: network latency to the cache — if the cache is in a separate AZ or remote on-prem instance, does that negate latency benefits?
[00:06:26] Carlos: yes placement matters. local co-location on the same host or same AZ is best. if you have a multi-region setup we'll recommend regional caches with async replication for warm pool pre-warm; live reads should be local to avoid extra RTT.
[00:06:40] Ravi: how big are typical prefix KV objects? we need to budget memory.
[00:06:44] Carlos: commonly a prefix KV per prompt is tens to a few hundred KB depending on model and sequence length. for LLMs with long context the KV can be larger. we provide tooling to estimate memory per prompt given model type and seq len distribution. in our experience, 1M cached prefixes might be several hundred GB, so quota planning is important.
[00:07:03] Angela: any special considerations for few-shot examples in the prefix? we sometimes include user-specific examples.
[00:07:08] Carlos: avoid caching user-specific examples unless you namespace them per-user and have quotas. for shared few-shot templates it's fine. you can also hybridize: cache the shared part, dynamically append the user-specific snippets at runtime (cheap compared to full KV recompute).
[00:07:23] [00:07:28] Priya: failure modes — if the cache returns stale prefix after model update, how do you invalidate?
[00:07:33] Carlos: include model_hash and rollout version in the cache key. when you roll a model, bump the model_hash and the cache entries will miss. we also support TTLs and a purge API that can invalidate prefixes by tag (e.g., model:v1.2).
[00:07:46] Ravi: what's the typical TTL we should set? minutes? hours? days?
[00:07:50] Carlos: TTL depends on how often your prompts or few-shot corpora change. for stable system prompts, days to weeks; for frequently edited templates, hours. start conservative: 24h TTL for pilot then adjust. monitor eviction/refresh rates.
[00:08:03] [00:08:10] Angela: are there cost tradeoffs? caching reduces per-token cost but increases memory storage cost. do you provide ROI estimators?
[00:08:16] Carlos: yes Redwood Optimize includes cost models: you input hit rates, average tokens saved per hit, storage cost per GB, and it outputs net savings. often for production chat use-cases caching pays back within weeks, especially with high QPS. we'll run a quick ROI with your traces.
[00:08:31] Sophia: one operational note: for Dedicated customers we expose per-route config to tune caching behavior and autoscaling to handle cache population spikes. for metra's expected throughput we recommend a Reserved capacity plan for predictable latency.
[00:08:45] Jon: for our on-prem pilot, can we do an initial POC with a small cache size and scale after we validate?
[00:08:50] Carlos: absolutely, start small. pre-warm the few most common prefixes and run the benchmark. we'll help calibrate the batch sizes and quantization profile to meet your P99 latency target.
[00:09:02] [00:09:08] Ravi: benchmarking — what does Redwood need from us?
[00:09:12] Carlos: three things: (1) anonymized request traces (sampled), (2) target latency SLOs and workload distribution (routes, QPS), (3) a small set of representative prompts. we'll run the benchmark against both Hosted match and Dedicated/private setup to show differences.
[00:09:27] Angela: privacy — when you say anonymized traces, what fields are essential?
[00:09:31] Carlos: we want prompt text (with PII removed or replaced by placeholders), timestamp, route id, and session markers. we don't need user identifiers; if you include them we'll hash client-side.
[00:09:42] [00:09:48] Priya: anything else we should be aware of before the pilot?
[00:09:51] Sophia: just to reiterate: include quant_profile in keys, namespace with tenant id, set conservative TTLs, pre-warm top N prefixes, and run A/B evals. we'll provide a config template and a linter for infra.
[00:10:05] Carlos: i'll also add: consider rate limits on pre-warm jobs so you don't thrash the runtime with a storm of cache fills; Redwood supports throttled pre-warm.
[00:10:15] Angela: great. would be good to see an example key format in the doc and a sample of the expected telemetry dashboards.
[00:10:22] Sophia: we'll include both.
[00:10:25] [wrap-up]
[00:10:28] Sophia: quick recap of agreed actions: we'll send the prefix-caching architecture doc, config template, and benchmark script. Metra will share traces and confirm VPC/KMS details. we'll schedule the 2-hour benchmark for week of May 26. any other questions?
[00:10:44] Angela: no, that's perfect. thanks.
[00:10:46] Jon: thanks everyone.
[00:10:48] Carlos: thanks, we'll follow up via email with links to docs and a calendar invite.
